Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 68, verse 1:

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Tafsir of Surat al-Qalam

It is Meccan according to the majority of scholars.

It is also reported from some of them that part of it is Meccan and part of it is Madani.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Nun﴾. There is disagreement regarding it. Mujahid said: it is the fish upon which the earths rest.

In the tafsir of al-Naqqash: all waters gush out from its jaws.

The second view: it is a name of the surah.

The third view: it is one of the letters of the alphabet used at the beginning of certain surahs (huruf al-tahajji, the disjointed letters).

It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that "Alif-Lam-Ra", "Ha-Mim", and "Nun" are a combination drawn from the name al-Rahman.

The fourth view: the nun is the inkwell (al-dawah). This is the view of al-Hasan and Qatadah. There is a transmitted report on the authority of Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Allah created first of all the pen. Then He created the nun, which is the inkwell. Then He said to the pen: Write.

It said: What shall I write? He said: Write what will happen and what has happened, of deeds, lifespans and provision until the Day of Resurrection.

So the pen wrote, and Allah sealed the mouth of the pen, so it does not speak, and will not speak until the Day of Resurrection. Then He created the intellect and said to it: I have not created a creature more wondrous to Me than you. By My might, I will perfect you in those whom I love, and I will diminish you in those whom I hate." Then the Prophet said: "The most complete of people in intellect are those most obedient to Allah and most active in His obedience, and the most deficient of people in intellect are those most obedient to Satan and most active in his obedience."

.

As for His saying ﴿wal-qalam﴾ (By the pen), it is said in tafsir that it was created from light, and its length is the distance between the heaven and the earth.

In the report of 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit, the Prophet said: "The first thing Allah created was the pen, and He said to it: Write. It said: What shall I write? He said: What will be until the Day of Resurrection."

There is disagreement concerning this inkwell and pen. The majority hold that it is the inkwell and the pen with which the Remembrance (al-Dhikr) was written in heaven.

The second view: it is the inkwell and the pen with which the children of Adam write.

The meaning of the verse is an oath, and Allah may swear by whatever He wills of His creation.

Qatadah said: were it not for the pen, no religion would stand for Allah, and creation would have no livelihood.

As for His saying ﴿wa ma yasturun﴾ (and what they inscribe), it means: what they write of the deeds of the children of Adam, meaning: the angels.

Al-Naqqash related from Ibn 'Abbas that disbelievers have no good deeds or bad deeds recorded for them; rather, that is recorded for believers, and the good deeds they do in this world, for which they are rewarded, and the bad deeds they do. Shirk is greater than all of that.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 68, verse 2:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿You are not, by the grace of your Lord, a madman.﴾ This is the place of the oath, and it is the answer to their saying, as Allah the Exalted related of them: ﴿And they say, "O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down, indeed you are a madman!"﴾.

And His words: ﴿by the grace of your Lord﴾ mean: by the mercy of your Lord.

It is also said: by His bestowal upon you. It is as if He negated madness from him by what Allah had bestowed upon him, just as a speaker says to another: "You are intelligent," or "You are wealthy, by the grace of Allah upon you."

And His saying: ﴿And indeed for you is a reward never cut off⁠—﴾ meaning: not interrupted.

It is also said: not reckoned (or not counted against you).

It is also said: not bestowed upon you as a favour that is held over you.

.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 68, verse 4:

And His saying: ﴿And indeed, you are of a great moral character﴾ means: upon the character with which God has disciplined you, namely that which the Qur'an has brought, such as doing good to people, pardoning, overlooking (wrongs), maintaining the ties of kinship, giving fairness (equity), enjoining what is right, forbidding what is wrong, and what is similar to that.

In the hadith of Sa'd ibn Hisham that he asked ʿĀ'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, about the character of the Prophet, and she said: "His character was the Qur'an."

That is: he was in accordance with what the Qur'an had brought.

And in another narration she said: "The Messenger of Allah was neither obscene nor one who spoke obscenely, nor did he repay an evil deed with its like, but rather he pardoned and forgave."

Al-Suddi said: ﴿And indeed, you are of a great moral character﴾ means: upon Islam.

Zayd ibn Aslam said: "upon a great religion," which is the religion that Allah the Exalted has approved for this community, and it is the most beloved of religions to Allah the Exalted.

It has also been related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Indeed Allah the Exalted created one hundred and seventeen characteristics; whoever comes with one of them enters Paradise."

And from him (ﷺ) that he said: "I was sent only to perfect the noble qualities of character."

It was also said: ﴿of a great moral character﴾ means: a noble disposition.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 68, verses 5–6:

His saying: ﴿So you will see, and they will see, which of you is the afflicted﴾. Abu 'Ubayda said: the "ba" (bi-) is extra (ṣila, a particle that adds no independent meaning).

Its meaning: "which of you is the afflicted" (al-maftun). He cited a line of poetry:

(We strike with the sword and hope for relief ...)

That is, "relief" (al-faraj).

As for al-Farra', al-Zajjaj and the rest of the grammarians (nahwiyyun), they did not accept this view. They mentioned two other opinions:

One of them: the meaning of His saying ﴿bi-ayyikum al-maftun﴾ is: "by which of you is the madness (al-fitna)". It is said: "Fulan has no ʿaql (reason) or jild (skin)," meaning, no reason and no hide.

The second opinion: "bi-ayyikum al-maftun" means "in which of you is the afflicted one", that is, (meaning) in the group in which the Messenger of God and his Companions are, or in the group in which Abu Jahl and his kin are.

The real meaning is: you will see on the Day of Resurrection and know that the madman was among you, not in the Messenger of God and his Companions, that is, in the group in which the Messenger of God and his Companions are.

Al-Nahhas also mentioned two opinions. He said: the meaning of His saying ﴿bi-ayyikum al-maftun﴾ is: "by which of you is the affliction of the afflicted," like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿wa-s'al al-qarya﴾ (and ask the town), that is, the people of the town.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 68, verses 5–6:

His saying: ﴿So you will see, and they will see, which of you is the afflicted﴾. Abu 'Ubayda said: the "ba" (bi-) is extra (ṣila, a particle that adds no independent meaning).

Its meaning: "which of you is the afflicted" (al-maftun). He cited a line of poetry:

That is, "relief" (al-faraj).

As for al-Farra', al-Zajjaj and the rest of the grammarians (nahwiyyun), they did not accept this view. They mentioned two other opinions:

One of them: the meaning of His saying ﴿bi-ayyikum al-maftun﴾ is: "by which of you is the madness (al-fitna)". It is said: "Fulan has no ʿaql (reason) or jild (skin)," meaning, no reason and no hide.

The second opinion: "bi-ayyikum al-maftun" means "in which of you is the afflicted one", that is, (meaning) in the group in which the Messenger of God and his Companions are, or in the group in which Abu Jahl and his kin are.

The real meaning is: you will see on the Day of Resurrection and know that the madman was among you, not in the Messenger of God and his Companions, that is, in the group in which the Messenger of God and his Companions are.

Al-Nahhas also mentioned two opinions. He said: the meaning of His saying ﴿bi-ayyikum al-maftun﴾ is: "by which of you is the affliction of the afflicted," like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿wa-s'al al-qarya﴾ (and ask the town), that is, the people of the town.
His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who has strayed from His way, and He is most knowing of those who are guided.﴾ The meaning is apparent.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 68, verse 8:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So do not obey the deniers﴾, meaning: the deniers of the signs of God.

Wa-qawluhu: "Waddu law tudhinu fayudhinun" means: they wish that you would be lax regarding your matter, so that they would be lax (in theirs), or that you would be gentle toward them, so that they would be gentle (toward you).

Al-mudahana (compromise) is outward companionship and courtesy, without agreement in the inner heart.

Al-Qutaybi (Ibn Qutaybah) said regarding the meaning of the verse: the disbelievers said to the Prophet, "We will worship your God with you for a period, and you worship our god with us for a period." This is the meaning of His words: "They wish that you would compromise, so they would compromise," meaning: you would incline toward their desire, so they would incline toward your desire.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 68, verse 10:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not obey every frequent swearer, contemptible﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: he is al-Walid ibn al-Mughira.

And from Mujahid: he is al-Aswad ibn 'Abd Yaghuth.

And from some of them: he is al-Akhnas ibn Shariq.

It has also been said: he refers generally (to anyone of this description).

His saying: ﴿every frequent swearer﴾, meaning: one who swears often.

His saying: ﴿contemptible﴾, meaning: despicable. Its meaning here is: lacking in judgment and discernment.

And His saying: ﴿Hammaz﴾, meaning: (ʿAtta) one who backbites and slanders people.

And His saying: ﴿Mashshaʾ bi-namim﴾, meaning: one who goes about with tale-bearing (al-namimah), which is conveying speech from one people to another.

It has been established from the Prophet (ﷺ) through the narration of Ḥudhayfah that he said: "The one who engages in qattat (tale-bearing) will not enter Paradise." That is, a nammam (tale-carrier).

And from him (ﷺ) that he said: "The most evil of people are those who go about with tale-bearing, who sow discord between friends, and who seek out the faults of the innocent."

And on the authority of Yaḥyā ibn Abī Kathīr, he said: "A tale-bearer can corrupt in a single day what a sorcerer cannot corrupt in a month."

And His saying: ﴿Hinderer of good﴾, meaning: stingy. It is also said: one who prevents (others) from Islam.

Al-Walid ibn al-Mughira used to say to his sons and his household: "Whoever among you embraces Islam, I will cut off from him my provision and my support."

And His saying: ﴿Transgressor﴾, meaning: one who exceeds the bounds in wrongdoing.

And His saying: ﴿Sinful﴾, meaning: one who commits much sin.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 68, verse 13:

His saying: ﴿ʿUtull﴾ means: the one of gross and foul character.

It is also said: the harsh, coarse one.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: one who does evil and is known for it.

Al-Naqqash transmitted it.

It is also related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Shall I not inform you of the people of the Fire? Every jaʿẓarī, jawwāẓ, ṣakhhāb in the markets, a corpse by night, a donkey by day, one who knows of this world but is ignorant of the Hereafter."

As for the jaʿẓarī, it means the one who eats much, drinks much, and is wrongful, and it is like the ʿutull.

Al-Jawwāẓ: it is the one who gathers and withholds, mentioned by Shaddad ibn Aws. Thaʿlab said: al-jawwāẓ is the one who is heavy in flesh and arrogant in his walk.

It is also said: "Fulan is jušš," meaning: large and bulky.

Among some strange reports it is related that the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "The sky weeps over a servant whose body Allah has made healthy, whose belly He has made wide, and whom He has given food to eat, and then he becomes a wrongdoer. And the sky weeps over an old adulterer, and the earth nearly cannot bear him."

His saying: ﴿Baʿda dhālika zanīm﴾ means: an illegitimate one (daʿī).

It is also said: one attached to the people while not being of them.

It is said: the one who has a zanama (mark) of evil by which he is recognized, like the zanama of a sheep.

Ḥassān said regarding the zanīm:

(A zanīm whom men claim, an addition, as the extra pieces are added to the breadth of the hide, the akārī'.)

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 68, verse 14:

The words of the Most High: ﴿Because he possesses wealth and sons﴾. It is also read: "أأن كان" (ʾa-ʾan kāna, with a question-marker before the first hamza).

So His words ﴿ʾan﴾ mean: because he possesses wealth and sons, he does such-and-such and says such-and-such; that is, on account of that.

And His words "أأن كان" mean: "Do not obey him, even though he possesses wealth and sons."

And His saying: ﴿When Our verses are recited to him, he says, "Tales of the ancients."﴾ We have already explained this.

Al-asatir (fables, tales) — its singular is usteera (usṭūrah).

Al-Kisa'i said: they are trivialities of speech, having no order or coherence.

The commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Qur'an) on Surah 68, verse 16:

And the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿We will brand him upon the snout﴾. Abu 'Ubayda, al-Mubarrad and others said: al-Khurtum (the snout) is the nose.

Its meaning: He will place upon his nose a mark by which he will be known to be one of the people of the Fire.

Jarir said:

(When I placed my branding-iron upon al-Farazdaq, and upon al-Bu'ayth I slit the nose of al-Akhtal.)

It is also said: the meaning of His words ﴿We will brand him upon the snout﴾ is: We will blacken his face, and the nose is described as the place of the face because it is part of it.

And it has been said: it will attach to him shame, disgrace, and something that will never leave him, ever.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 68, verse 17:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, We have tested them﴾, meaning: the people of Makkah. This was when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) supplicated and said: "O Allah, make it upon them years like the years of Yusuf." So they were struck by hunger until they ate al-'Ilhiz (a paste made of blood and plant matter) and burnt bones.

And His saying: ﴿as We tested the people of the garden﴾. In most of the exegeses, it is said that this was an old man in Yemen who had sons, and who owned an orchard from which he gave charity to the poor, and from which he spent on himself and his children.

It is also said: he would give a third in charity, spend a third on himself and his children, and return a third to the upkeep of the garden. When the old man died, his sons said: "The dependents are many, and the income is small, and it does not suffice for giving to the poor." So they agreed to go to the orchard at dawn, while it was still dark, and cut its fruit and harvest before the poor could know.

The poor had become accustomed to attending the harvesting and cutting. So when they had agreed upon this, Allah, may He be exalted, sent a fire from the sky that night, and the orchard and its trees were burned. It is also said that this man was a man from Thaqif.

And His saying: ﴿when they swore﴾, meaning: they took oaths.

And His saying: ﴿that they would surely harvest it in the morning﴾, meaning: they would cut it at the time we have mentioned.
And His saying: ﴿And they did not make exception﴾, i.e., they did not say: "If God wills."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 68, verse 19:

And His saying: ﴿Then there passed over it a visitation from your Lord﴾, meaning: a visitor came upon it from the punishment, and it was the fire that Allah the Exalted had sent.

The Arabs do not use the word ṭā'if (visitation, something passing by in the night) except in reference to punishment.

And in some of the exegetical works: Allah the Exalted commanded an angel, who uprooted that garden with its trees and plantings and placed it in the location of what is today the Ṭā'if (a city in the Hijaz).

And His saying: ﴿while they were sleeping﴾, we have mentioned it.

"His saying: ﴿So it became like a darkened night﴾ — i.e., like a dark night.

It is also said: like a day in which there is nothing.

The Arabs call a cultivated land "day" (nahar) because of its whiteness (bayad), and a barren, neglected land "night" (layl) because of its blackness and greenness.

Al-sarim (الصريم) is among the words with opposite meanings (al-adhdad); it is a name for both night and day together, because each of them cuts off (yaqta'u) the other from its companion.

It is also said: "like al-sarim" means al-masrum (the harvested/cut-off), with the form fa'il used in the sense of maf'ul; that is, nothing remained in it."
And His saying: ﴿So they called out to one another at dawn﴾. That is, some of them called to others at the time of morning.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 68, verse 22:

And His saying: ﴿Go early to your tilth﴾, meaning: make for your tilth (aqsidu harthakum).

And in the narrative: they had tilled fields and vineyards.

And His saying: ﴿if you are going to harvest﴾, meaning: cutting off (qati'in).

It is said: for grapes it is al-siram (sarram), and for crops it is al-hasad (harvesting).

The poet said:

(I went to him in the morning and found him, / sitting over him at al-Sarim were his blamers)

Here, al-sarim is the black night (al-jarrah al-sawda').

Ibn Faris also mentioned it in the meaning of al-sarim that we mentioned earlier.

And it is reported from Ibn Juraij that he said: a flame of fire came out from the middle of their valley and burned their garden.

And His saying: ﴿if you are going to harvest﴾ — Mujahid said: what is meant by it is the harvesting of grapes.

And their tilth was grapes.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 68, verses 23–24:

His words, ﴿So they set off, speaking in low voices﴾: i.e., they spoke secretly and furtively. And their speech was, ﴿No needy person shall enter it upon you today﴾: i.e., do not let the needy [*yadkhulūna*, "enter"] upon you.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 68, verses 23–24:

His words, ﴿So they set off, speaking in low voices﴾: i.e., they spoke secretly and furtively. And their speech was, ﴿No needy person shall enter it upon you today﴾: i.e., do not let the needy [*yadkhulūna*, "enter"] upon you.

And their saying: ﴿And they set out early, determined﴾ — the most well-known of the opinions is that its meaning is "with jealousy" (ḥasad), which is the view of Qatadah, Mujahid, al-Hasan and a group.

It is also reported from al-Sha'bi and Sufyan that they said: "with anger" — that is, against the poor.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: "ʿalā ḥardin" means "with prevention" (manʿ). It is said: the year (sanah) was barren (ḥāradat al-sanah), so there was no rain in it; and the she-camel was barren (ḥāradat al-nāqah) when she had no milk.

The meaning of prevention is what they had agreed upon: preventing the poor.

It is reported from al-Hasan, in one narration: "with eagerness" (ḥirṣ).

It was also said: "with intention" (qaṣd).

The poet said:

(A torrent came from the command of God... it intends with the intention of a garden that has been cut off)

That is, it intends.

It is reported from al-Suddi that ḥard was the name of their garden.

And his saying: ﴿capable﴾ means: capable in their own estimation of harvesting.

It was also said: "capable" means: over a matter they had established among themselves.

Almost. The Arabic passage is short, and I'll translate it as it stands.

God Most High said: ﴿So when they saw it, they said, "Indeed, we have certainly gone astray."﴾ He means: when they saw the place of the garden, and there was in it no tree and no plant, they said, "Indeed, we have certainly gone astray," that is, "We have missed the way to our garden."

And His saying: ﴿Rather, we are deprived﴾ means: they became alert to the matter and realized that they had not gone astray on the way, so they said: "Rather, we are deprived," that is: the punishment has descended and we have been deprived of the fruits of our garden.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 68, verse 28:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Said the most moderate of them﴾, meaning: the best of them and the most just.

Similar to this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation﴾, meaning: just, excellent.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the most intelligent of them.

And His saying: ﴿Did I not tell you, "Why do you not glorify [God]?"﴾, meaning: Why did you not say, "If God wills"?

Glorification (tasbih) was placed here in the position of the will (mashi'ah), because tasbih is the declaring of God far above every evil.

And His saying "if God wills" contains the meaning of declaring Him free of imperfection, which is that no one owns the ability to do anything except by His will; so He is exalted above anything being in His dominion except what He wills.

And from 'Ikrimah: their exception was the tasbih, meaning: they used to say, in place of our saying "if God wills," "Glory be to God" (subhan Allah).
They said: ﴿Glory be to our Lord! Indeed we were wrongdoers.﴾ That is: by withholding from the poor.

And His saying: ﴿So they turned upon one another, blaming each other﴾. That is: some of them blame others, so one says to the other: "It was you who did it, and the fault is yours," and the other says to his companion the same.

And His saying, ﴿They said, "O woe to us!"﴾: they invoked woe (al-waylu) upon themselves.

And His saying, ﴿Indeed we were transgressors (ṭāghīn)﴾: meaning, wrongdoers (ẓālimīn).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 68, verse 32:

As for His words, ﴿Perhaps our Lord will give us in exchange something better than it﴾, this is a report of their repentance and remorse, and of their asking Allah, exalted is He, to replace their garden for them with something better than it, so that they would give the rightful due of the needy (al-masakin).

And in some of the tafsirs: that Allah, exalted is He, accepted their repentance and gave them a garden better than it.

And Allah knows best.

As for His words, ﴿Indeed, we are turning to our Lord, desiring [His mercy]﴾, meaning: by our asking.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 68, verse 33:

And His words: ﴿Such is the punishment﴾, meaning: such is the punishment of this world.

And His words: ﴿But the punishment of the Hereafter is greater, if they only knew﴾, meaning: the punishment of the Hereafter.

It is also said: Just as We punished these people and brought down (punishment) upon them, so too do We punish Quraysh and bring it down upon them.

It has been related in the tafsir that Allah the Exalted sent down punishment upon them on the day of Badr. When they set out for Badr, they said: "We will surely kill them, and we will surely kill Muhammad (ﷺ), and we will surely take them captive, and we will return to Makkah, circumambulate the House, shave our heads, drink wine, and have singing-girls (al-qiyan) play music over our heads." They swore to this, but Allah made their assumption false, and there befell them what befell them of killing and captivity.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, for the righteous with their Lord are the Gardens of Bliss.﴾ When He mentioned the punishment of the disbelievers and what He would bring down upon them, He mentioned what He had promised to the believers in this verse. It is related that ʿUtba ibn Rabiʿa said when this verse was revealed: "If Allah gives you the Gardens of Bliss in the Hereafter, then He will give us the like of what He gives you, or better than it."

Then God Most High sent down: ﴿Shall We then treat the Muslims like the criminals?﴾ That is: Shall We make the Muslims equal to the polytheists in granting the gardens of bliss? It is mentioned in the manner of a rebuke, meaning: He does not do such a thing.
Its meaning: "What is wrong with you? How do you judge?" That is, how do you pass judgment? The intended sense of "judging" here is their judgment about themselves, that they will have Paradise.

Its (Allah's) saying: ﴿Or do you have a Book in which you study?﴾ That is, you study what you judge by.

It is also said: you repeatedly examine it, and so you judge from it for yourselves whatever you judge.
In his commentary on the verse, al-Sam'ani says: "And His saying: ﴿Indeed, for you therein is whatever you choose﴾, meaning: whatever you select; and this is an explanation of that ruling."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 68, verse 39:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Or do you have oaths binding upon Us, extending to the Day of Resurrection?﴾ That is: emphatic (muakkada). The meaning of "bāligha" (extending, reaching its limit) in the speech of the Arabs in such contexts is: reaching the utmost limit. It is said: "This is a good thing, bāligh," meaning it has reached the utmost limit in goodness.

And His saying: ﴿to the Day of Resurrection﴾ means: continuance and permanence. It has also been said: "Do you have emphatic oaths that We will not punish you until the Day of Resurrection?"

And His saying: ﴿That you shall have what you judge﴾ is an explanation of what the oath was made about.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Qur'an) on surah 68, verse 40:

And His saying: ﴿Ask them which of them will stand surety for that.﴾ That is: guarantor (kafil).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 68, verse 41:

His words: ﴿Or do they have partners?﴾ This is on the basis of a broad usage of speech (tawassu' al-kalam).

Its meaning: with them, and in their claim.

It has also been said: "Or do the partners bear witness to this," with shuhada' (witnesses) understood as the meaning of shuraka' (partners), as mentioned by al-Naqqash.

.

His words: ﴿So let them bring their partners, if they are truthful﴾. That is: bring partners who belong to them according to their claim, on the first opinion; and on the second opinion, bring their testimonies, if they are truthful.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 68, verse 42:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿On the Day when the shin is uncovered﴾. ʿIkrima reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: "[It means] the severe matter." In another narration from Ibn ʿAbbas, he said: "If the Qur'an becomes unclear to you, then seek its meaning in poetry, for it is the register (dīwān) of the Arabs." And he recited:

("The war stood upon us on a shin..." )

This is a well-known saying. Ibn Qutayba said: When the Arabs faced a severe matter, they expressed it with this wording, because a person who faces a matter and takes it up with seriousness and effort says, "He rolled up his shin (shammara ʿan sāqihi)," so the shin was placed in the position of hardship.

The poet said:

("A brother of war: if war bites him, he bites back; and if war rolls up its shin, he rolls up too.")

And Duraid ibn al-Simma said:

("Short of waist-wrapper, his shin exposed to half its length, patient against the harsh one, a climber of the steep.")

In another narration from Ibn ʿAbbas: "On the Day when the shin is uncovered" means: on a day of terror, distress and hardship, and this has the same meaning as the first.

Mujahid said: It is the first hour of the hours of the Resurrection, the most dreadful and severe of them for the people.

All of this is one opinion.

Abu Saʿid al-Khudri narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, our Lord will uncover His shin, and every believing man and woman will prostrate. The hypocrites will go to prostrate but they will not be able to."

Ibn Masʿud also reported something similar to this.

Al-Hasan al-Basri said: "On the Day when the shin is uncovered" means: the veil between this world and the Hereafter.

It is also said: the covering between this world and the Hereafter; the two meanings are close.

His saying: ﴿And they are called to prostration, but they will not be able﴾ means: the hypocrites will not be able to prostrate.

In the report: "Their spines will become rigid (fa-yaʿqimu aṣlābahum)," meaning the spines of the hypocrites. His saying "yaʿqim" means: it becomes one single layer.

In another narration: "It becomes like a piece of iron (kisf qayd al-ḥadīd)."

In the report narrated by Abu Musa al-Ashʿari from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, every people will be shown what they used to worship in the world, and they will follow it. The people of monotheism (ahl al-tawḥīd) will remain, and it will be said to them: The people have gone, so what are you waiting for? They will say: Indeed, for us there is a Lord whom we used to worship.

It will be said to them: Would you recognize Him if you saw Him? They will say: Yes.

It will be said: How will you recognize Him when you have not seen Him? They will say: Indeed, He has no likeness.

Then the veil will be lifted for them, and every believing man and woman will prostrate, while the hypocrites will remain and be unable to prostrate, and their backs will become like the horns of cows (ṣiyāṣ al-baqar).

Then God, may He be exalted, will say to the believers: Lift up your heads, for I have placed in the Fire, in place of every man among you, a man from the Jews and Christians."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 68, verse 43:

And His saying: ﴿their eyes will be humbled﴾, meaning: their eyes are humiliated, and what is intended by this is the humiliation of regret and anguish.

And His saying: ﴿humiliation will cover them﴾, meaning: disgrace and degradation overwhelm them.

And His saying: ﴿and they used to be called to prostration while they were sound﴾, meaning: they were called to the congregational prayer while they were sound, that is, healthy and free from affliction. And now prostration is for them (mahyat).

.

The apparent meaning of the verse is that its meaning is prostration in the prayer (salah).

It is reported from Ibrahim al-Taymi that he said: it is the prescribed prayer (al-salah al-maktubah).

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: they were called to prostration with "hayya 'ala'l-falah" (come to success), while they were sound, so they did not respond.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 68, verse 44:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿So leave Me with those who deny this discourse﴾ mean: leave Me with them and with it, and entrust them to Me, for I will recompense them for their deeds.

It is also said: "Leave Me" means: do not occupy your heart with it; leave Me with them, for I am the one who will requite them and repay them, and this has the same meaning as the first.

The Arabs say the like of this statement even when there is no one present to prevent him from it. The poet said:

(Leave me with the fox, O Umm Sa'd... the earth carries me (or your house) and I am carried away)

As for His words: ﴿We will draw them on step by step from where they do not know﴾, istidraj (gradual drawing on) in the speech of the Arabs means taking little by little, and from it comes "the child crawled (daraja) when he walked little by little."

'Abd al-Rahman ibn Dawud al-Khuraybi narrated from Sufyan al-Thawri that he said: istidraj is the lavishing of blessings together with the withholding of gratitude.

It is also said: it is that whenever they commit a sin, Allah renews a blessing for them.

From 'Uqba ibn Muslim, who said: When a servant is in disobedience to Allah and then Allah gives him what he loves, let him know that he is under istidraj.

From al-Hasan al-Basri, who said: How many a person drawn on gradually is praised for his goodness, and how many a deluded one is covered by Allah's concealment.

It is also said: "We will draw them on step by step" means: We will plot against them from where they do not know.

And His saying: ﴿And I give them respite﴾, meaning: I grant them time and do not seize them suddenly and openly, but I take them little by little and deal with them by stratagem, gradually.

We have already explained the meaning of respite (al-imhal) and granting time (al-imla') earlier.

And His saying: ﴿Indeed, My plan is firm﴾, meaning: strong.

Al-Sam'ani's commentary on surah 68, verse 46:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Or do you ask them for a reward, so that they are burdened with debt?﴾ That is: a reward for conveying the message, so that they are weighed down by debt.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 68, verse 47:

And His saying: ﴿Or do they have the unseen, so that they write (it down)?﴾ That is: they have the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz) with them. He called it "the unseen" because what is hidden from the servants is written in it.

And His saying: ﴿So that they write (it down)﴾ That is: they write from it whatever they judge in their own favor and what accords with their desires.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 68, verse 48:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿So be patient with the decision of your Lord, and do not be like the companion of the fish﴾, meaning: in impatience and in abandoning patience.

It is also said: "Do not be wrathful as the companion of the fish was wrathful," and he is Dhu'l-Nun (the Possessor of the Fish), whose name is Yunus ibn Matta, may the blessings of Allah be upon him.

And His words: ﴿when he cried out while he was distressed﴾, meaning: filled with anguish and grief.

It is also said: "Kazama al-ba'ir bi-jirratih" (the camel held in its cud) when it withholds it, and the meaning is that he found no outlet or passage for the grief that was in his heart, so he suppressed it (kazama 'alayhi), meaning he held it in.

And His saying: ﴿Had not a blessing from his Lord reached him﴾ means: a mercy from his Lord.

And His saying: ﴿he would have been cast out onto the open plain﴾ — al-'arā' is the surface of the earth.

It is also said: it is the open, exposed place.

And His saying: ﴿while he was blameworthy﴾ means: he would have been cast out not blameworthy; but had it not been for the mercy of his Lord, he would have been blameworthy.

God's words, "But his Lord chose him" (﴿فاجتباه ربه﴾), mean: He selected him and preferred him.

God's words, "And made him among the righteous" (﴿فجعله من الصالحين﴾), mean: among His righteous servants.

We have already mentioned his story before.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 68, verse 51:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed, those who disbelieve would almost make you slip with their eyes﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas recited: "yuzhiqunaka bi-absarihim" (they would make you perish with their eyes). Al-zalq is falling, and al-izlaq is causing to fall.

There are two well-known opinions regarding the verse. The first: "they would make you slip with their eyes," meaning they would afflict you with the evil eye (ya'tanunaka), and its meaning is that they would strike you with their eyes.

This was mentioned by al-Kalbi, Muqatil and others, and al-Farra' also mentioned it in his book.

It is narrated that a man among the Arabs would starve himself for three days, then go out, and a camel or sheep of his neighbour would pass by him, so he would say: "How fine it is, how large it is, how fat it is," and similar things; then it would fall down from among them the number [of its kind], and be destroyed.

In some tafsirs it is mentioned that this was among the Banu Asad of the Arabs, and a man would afflict with the evil eye the camel or sheep of one of them, then say to his servant: "Go with a basket and a dirham, so that you may take for us from its meat." He would be certain that it would fall, and then it would be slaughtered.

The second opinion regarding the verse, which is the better of the two, is that what is meant by it is that they look at you with a gaze of hatred and enmity, so that from the intensity of their gaze they almost overthrow you, that is, they bring you down and cast you to the ground. This is in accordance with the manner of Arabic speech.

The Arabs say: "So-and-so gazed a gaze that nearly felled him or devoured him," or "So-and-so looked at me a look that nearly felled me, or nearly devoured me with it," meaning: if he were able to fell me or devour me with it, he would fell me or devour me.

This is the choice of al-Zajjaj and others among the scholars of the meanings (ahl al-ma'ani).

They recited:

(They glance at one another when they meet in a battlefield, with a gaze that would remove the feet from their places)

His saying: ﴿when they hear the Reminder﴾, that is, the Qur'an, and their enmity and hatred would intensify when they heard it being recited.

His saying: ﴿and they say: "Indeed he is a madman"﴾, a name they called him by.

And His saying: ﴿It is nothing but a reminder to the worlds﴾ means: an honour to the worlds. It is a kinayah (a figurative reference) to the Messenger.

The more apparent view is that the Qur'an is a reminder to the worlds.

It has also been said: the Messenger is one who reminds the worlds. We have already explained the meaning of al-'Alamin (the worlds) earlier.
